messages.content:
I am working on this school project where I'm learning how to differentiate between various machine learning models used in artificial intelligence. In this repo that we're working in are my notes, and in here I actually have a reference stock, which is the PDF of the first chapter. This should have some really good reference documentation for us to go against and verify.

I don't want those to be the only source, but if we do leverage other sources via WebFetch or anything like that, we should make sure that we document where the details of that came from. That is especially because I'm going to be using this to eventually write a journal, and this is strictly the research side of this work.

Assume I don't know anything about AI, assume I know nothing about algorithms and machine learning and deep learning, and assume I know none of it. I need to learn it pretty much as quickly as possible, almost as if this was a spike and I needed to really dive in and learn the details as a junior. That is really the goal there, because I need to learn this stuff so that, down the line, when I grow in this class, I need to have the foundations down, and these are the foundations.

I really want to make sure we do well with this. I've got some notes all throughout this repo, stuff like using analogies. I used to be a big World of Warcraft player. I know a little bit about old-school RuneScape. I like analogies that go against video games that did really well for me when I was learning C# for the very first time and interfaces. I used to say, "Your character would have an interface, and the interface would be the class and all those things," stuff like that.

We don't have to always use it, but the simpler we can break things down and make it easy to understand is key. I like smaller files, many organized and structured. That's my vibe.

Got it. I’ll treat this repository as a beginner-friendly research notebook, not as a place to generate polished journal prose prematurely.

I inspected the current structure and the 80-page Chapter 1 PDF. The existing organization fits your preferences well:

- `findings.md` acts as the weekly index and review sheet.
- `findings/` holds small, focused concept notes.
- `sources/` contains the reference material.
- `journal.md` remains separate from the research notes.

For future work, I’ll follow these rules:

- Explain every concept from zero assumed knowledge.
- Introduce terminology only after explaining the underlying idea.
- Use WoW, RuneScape, and software analogies when they genuinely clarify something.
- Always include where an analogy breaks down.
- Keep notes small, linked, and organized by one main question per file.
- Distinguish easily confused terms such as algorithm, model, training, prediction, classification, and regression.
- Cite the chapter by PDF page number.
- Clearly cite and link any external sources.
- Prefer primary sources and official documentation for technical verification.
- Flag disagreements, oversimplifications, or potentially outdated claims in the textbook.
- Include retrieval questions so you can test whether you understand something without looking.

The chapter provides enough material to begin with this learning sequence:

1. AI, machine learning, neural networks, and deep learning
2. Algorithms versus trained models
3. Features, labels, training, validation, and prediction
4. Classification versus regression
5. Major learning approaches
6. Individual model families
7. How to select and compare models
8. Neural networks and deep learning

Your two focused findings files are currently almost empty and untracked, so those are the natural starting point. The strongest first unit would be `machine-learning-models.md`, beginning with the vocabulary needed to understand what a “model” actually is before comparing specific model types.

I'm thinking we get started with the first thing: differentiating between various machine learning models used in artificial intelligence and understanding the differences between them. I know there are differences in types of models. When you talk about frontier models, you have models like Claude Sonnet 4.8, Opus 4.8, or Sonnet 5, which are your frontier models, your heavy hitters, and your more everyday kind of use.

You also have your new Fayable 5, which is your super secure model. The architecture on that is really interesting because the model talks to another model to make sure you're not breaking rules. That is really interesting in the way that they have that architecture. You have models that recently came out, like 5.6 Salt, which I don't really know much about, but I know that's an open AI's frontier model. You have open weight models, which are things like Gemma 4 and stuff like that.

I have a rough idea that those are really open source, where you can run it locally wherever you want, but you don't have the training data and stuff like that. Those are what I understand when it comes to various machine learning models, but I think there's more here that I don't know of. What you don't know is what you don't know, so I just want to really have that strong foundation there.

That's going to be the biggest thing with working with you as a model. I want to understand and really learn, but I also need to make sure that what you're providing me is right and not incorrect, because AI can make mistakes, and I want to make sure this is correct.

How does that all come together in something like building my own model?
The reason why I asked this is because I think this will help me bring a lot of this home for me. It's probably going to have a little bit of ML in there, right, because you're going to have that machine learning to do the predictability for the next character. You're also going to have a little bit of some deep learning in there, because you need to have an extensive layer research of all the different frontends. I work for an enterprise, right? They own multiple different business units, multiple different pieces. I would want to think of scale: how would I train this model to work with all of our business units?
Now, I might start it off with just one because that's an easier feat, but I just want to tie these learnings together. I want a really step-by-step breakdown and a really, really simplified, kindergarten-grade explanation of what this would look like and how it worked, just so that I can have the high level and understand it and really tie back what I'm learning here.
I think a lot of this is really interesting, right? You would use that deep layer, kind of really, to get into the business unit pieces. I think it's interesting that I've always thought that machine learning and AI were always involved, right? You're kind of saying here that it could just be an algorithm, and that's something I never even thought about, right? I always assumed there was ML involved and stuff like that. The note provides:

The central conclusion is:

> You probably would not begin by creating a new model. You would build a governed AI system around an existing model, retrieve the correct UI documentation, validate its output mechanically, measure its failures, and only then decide whether changing model weights is worthwhile.

I also linked the note from `findings.md`.
Now, does this example use an existing model like Clog or Chat, or is this building our own foundational model within the whole system?

This example uses an existing foundation model—such as Claude, GPT, or an open-weight coding model—as the starting point.

You would not initially build your own foundation model.

There are three increasingly difficult meanings of “our own model”:

1. Existing model with company context: use Claude or GPT and provide retrieved company documentation. No weights change.
2. Customized open-weight model: download an existing foundation model such as Gemma or gpt-oss and fine-tune some of its weights, possibly using LoRA. You now have a customized UI model, but the underlying language ability came from the original foundation model.
3. New foundation model from scratch: start with untrained parameters and teach the model language, programming, reasoning, and UI generation through massive-scale pretraining.

The third option is far beyond what this example proposes. The likely progression would be Claude/GPT plus retrieval, then a smaller or open-weight model plus retrieval, then a fine-tuned open-weight model if justified.

So you would be building your own AI system, potentially your own customized model, but not your own foundation model.

Got it. Yeah, I've done the system already. I did that at work. We have a really strong foundation for that. What I'm more interested in is having our own foundation model, really, because that's the part I don't really understand.

Building a Kodak Cod code-optimized project is pretty straightforward nowadays. You would do that with Claude.md, and you just give it the correct context packs and all those things. You make things really, really structured in a way where you try to make things as deterministic as possible.

What I'm interested in is the foundational model itself, because the foundational model would eliminate cost, right? That's what I'm looking for. I'm looking to eliminate cost.

No—a foundation model would not eliminate cost. It would eliminate or reduce the vendor’s API bill while moving the cost onto your company.

A hosted model has API charges and integration work. A self-hosted model has GPU hardware or cloud costs, electricity, storage, serving, training, engineers, monitoring, and upgrades. OpenAI explicitly notes that open-weight operators remain responsible for compute, storage, hosting, and maintenance costs.

What you likely want is a small, company-controlled coding model that is inexpensive to run and highly capable within a narrow frontend domain. That is probably a domain-specific model rather than a new foundation model.

The three realistic options are:

1. Train a foundation model from scratch. This provides maximum ownership but the highest upfront cost, and inference still costs money.
2. Continue pretraining an open-weight foundation model on a large company-approved code corpus. This creates a company-specialized base model while retaining general abilities.
3. Fine-tune or distill a smaller open-weight model. This is the most realistic cost-reduction experiment. The inexpensive internal model can handle repetitive work while difficult requests escalate to a frontier model.

The correct comparison is cost per accepted prototype, including infrastructure, engineering, corrections, and operations—not merely token price.

The recommended research question is: Can a small open-weight coding model be trained to generate accepted prototypes at a lower total cost than the current Claude workflow?

A new foundation model gives maximum ownership but enormous cost. A small, specialized derivative of an open-weight foundation model is much more likely to reduce total prototype-generation cost.

Got it, but what if I took something like Gemma, which is open-source, and I can download the weight, right? I can run that locally. What if I were to take that and leverage that as the baseline for teaching base architecture, right? All those core pieces, like how to code all those things. I took that model as the base and wrapped all of our stuff around it to create my own open-weighted model. Is that even possible? What does that look like? Stuff like that.

Yes. That is possible and is likely the kind of model project you mean.

You would take Gemma’s existing architecture and pretrained weights, continue training or fine-tune those weights using authorized company data, evaluate the result, and deploy the resulting derivative model yourself. You would not create the original foundation from nothing; you would create your own derivative model built on a foundation model.

Gemma is generally described by Google as an open model with open weights. Whether a particular release qualifies as open source depends on its exact license. Google’s terms call modified Gemma models Model Derivatives.

Three implementations are possible:

1. Wrapper only: unchanged Gemma weights plus prompts, RAG, tools, and documents. This is a new system but not a newly trained model.
2. LoRA adapter: frozen Gemma weights plus a small set of newly trained adapter weights.
3. Merged or fully fine-tuned derivative: merge an adapter into the base or directly train some or all original parameters, producing a derivative checkpoint.

You normally do not teach the architecture. The architecture is the blueprint; training changes the weights inside that blueprint. Gemma already supplies the architecture, tokenizer, general knowledge, coding ability, and pretrained weights. Your training specializes the weights.

A realistic pipeline is:

1. Choose a Gemma starting checkpoint.
2. Establish an unmodified baseline.
3. Prepare continued-pretraining data from approved code and technical material.
4. Prepare supervised input/output examples.
5. Keep evaluation data separate.
6. Begin with LoRA.
7. Evaluate build success, component validity, accessibility, visual acceptance, latency, and total cost.
8. Preserve the adapter or merge it into a derivative checkpoint.
9. Quantize for lower inference requirements.
10. Deploy it through an internally controlled inference service.

Publishing the weights would require compliance with the Gemma license and authorization to expose anything learned from enterprise data. An internally owned derivative of an open-weight base is often more realistic than a publicly released model.

The clearest description is: a domain-specialized derivative language model created by continuing to train and fine-tune an existing open-weight Gemma foundation model on authorized enterprise frontend data.

Love that. Let's take that idea and update the making-a-ui-model.md to reflect that play, just to understand what that would look like at a high level, something I can come back to some time later and noodle on. Maybe that becomes my capstone project at the end of this degree.

The note now preserves two distinct approaches:

1. The production-system approach already built.
2. The capstone model-building approach, where a Gemma adapter or derivative checkpoint is trained and tested to determine whether changing weights improves quality or cost over retrieval alone.
